name: Bulgarian State Championship
content:
Before 1948, Bulgarian football did not have a unified national league system. Instead, the championship—established in 1924—was organized as a knockout-style national tournament. Clubs first competed in regional divisions, and the regional winners advanced to a playoff stage to determine the national champion.

This structure reflected the early development of football in Bulgaria, where the sport was still semi-organized and heavily localized. Regional football associations played a key role, and clubs often had uneven levels of competition due to geographical separation. As a result, the national title was decided over relatively few matches compared to modern league systems.

Although this format helped spread football across the country, it lacked consistency and regular high-level competition. By the late 1940s, the need for a centralized league became clear, especially as football in Europe was moving toward more structured, season-long competitions. This led to the creation of a proper national league system in 1948.

name: First Professional Football League
content:
In 1948, Bulgaria introduced the A Republican Football Group, the first true national league, marking the beginning of continuous league-format championships. The system was heavily influenced by the Soviet model, including experiments with spring–autumn seasons and frequent structural changes. The number of teams often varied, and reforms—including club mergers—were common, especially during the communist period.

During the socialist era, football clubs were often tied to state institutions such as the army, police, or industries. This led to dominant teams like CSKA and Levski, as well as politically influenced reorganizations of clubs and competitions. Despite instability in format, the league became the central pillar of Bulgarian football and remained the top level of competition throughout the second half of the 20th century.

After the fall of communism, the league gradually transitioned into a modern professional system. It underwent multiple rebrandings and reforms, eventually becoming the First Professional Football League in 2016. Today, it operates with promotion and relegation, UEFA qualification spots, and a structure aligned with European standards, continuing the legacy of the national championship that began in 1924.

name: Tsar's Cup
content:
The Tsar’s Cup was the first official national cup competition in Bulgaria, introduced in 1938 during the monarchy period of the Kingdom of Bulgaria. It functioned as a knockout tournament and coexisted with the national championship, giving clubs an additional opportunity to compete for a major national trophy. The format followed a classic elimination system, with matches played over single legs or occasionally replays.

This competition represented one of the earliest attempts to establish a structured domestic cup in Bulgarian football. It brought together clubs from different regions, similar to the pre-1948 championship system, and helped increase nationwide interest in the sport. Winning the Tsar’s Cup was considered a prestigious achievement, though it did not yet carry the same long-term continuity as later competitions.

The tournament was discontinued after 1944 following major political changes in Bulgaria, including the end of the monarchy. As the country transitioned into a socialist state, football structures were reorganized, and the Tsar’s Cup was replaced by new competitions aligned with the ideology and organization of the communist regime.

name: Soviet Army Cup
content:
The Soviet Army Cup was established in 1946 and became the primary national cup competition during the socialist era in People's Republic of Bulgaria. It was heavily influenced by Soviet sporting structures, both in name and organization, reflecting the political alignment of the country at the time. The tournament followed a knockout format and involved clubs from across all divisions.

For decades, the Soviet Army Cup was regarded as the main domestic cup trophy in Bulgaria. Clubs such as CSKA Sofia and Levski Sofia frequently dominated the competition, mirroring their success in the league. The cup provided an additional route to silverware and often carried significant prestige, especially in a system where state-backed clubs held strong influence.

From the early 1980s, however, its status began to shift. A parallel competition—the Bulgarian Cup—was introduced and gradually took precedence. For several years, both tournaments existed simultaneously, creating a somewhat confusing hierarchy. By 1990, following the fall of communism, the Soviet Army Cup was abolished, ending its role as a major national competition.

name: Bulgarian Cup
content:
The Bulgarian Cup was introduced in 1981 and eventually became the country’s primary domestic cup competition. Initially, it existed alongside the Soviet Army Cup, but it quickly gained importance and recognition, especially as Bulgarian football began to modernize in the late socialist period. The competition adopted a standard knockout format, similar to other European domestic cups.

During the transitional years of the 1980s, both cups were contested, but the Bulgarian Cup increasingly became the more prestigious of the two. After 1990, it officially replaced the Soviet Army Cup as the main national knockout tournament. It also became the competition through which Bulgarian clubs could qualify for European tournaments, further increasing its significance.

In the modern era, the Bulgarian Cup remains a central part of the domestic football calendar. It includes clubs from all professional and many amateur levels, maintaining the traditional knockout spirit. Today, it operates alongside the First Professional Football League (Bulgaria) and continues to provide opportunities for both top teams and underdogs to achieve national success.
